title: Conversation runtime primer + stream rescue paths
next_steps: Send security pack + SOC2 cert link
Share sandbox access and quickstart notes
Schedule pilot benchmark next week (Devon + Marcus)
action_items: Marcus: run 1k-message latency benchmark on their sample workload by 2025-08-20
Lydia: email pricing tiers and Dedicated capacity options by 2025-08-15
Marta: review KMS/HSM integration doc and confirm compliance questions by 2025-08-19
summary: Introductory demo of Redwood hosted conversation runtime. Focus on streaming behaviour, tuning parameters (temperature, max_tokens, top_p), and retries/fallbacks. Customer has latency and compliance concerns; we agreed next steps for a pilot and security review.
transcript:
[00:00] Lydia (Redwood AE): Hey everybody, thanks for carving out time. Quick intros?
[00:07] Sara (Quantify Labs): Hi I'm Sara, eng manager, quick note we run a customer-facing chat assistant and latency is kinda the top metric for us.
[00:14] Devon: Devon here, backend, we'll likely own integration.
[00:17] Marta: Marta, security. I'll ask the usual compliance questions.
[00:21] Lydia: Great, Marcus (SE) will do the demo, I'll jump in on pricing and next steps. Marcus?
[00:27] Marcus (Redwood SE): Cool, hi all. Goal for today: show how the hosted runtime streams tokens, what settings change quality vs cost, and how retries/fallbacks work in practice. I'll start in the Console sandbox then switch to a tiny curl demo.
[00:40] Marcus: First, high level: our conversation API streams deltas as tokens are generated. That means clients can render incremental text and cancel early to save tokens. We do continuous KV cache reuse for multi-turn.
[00:55] Devon: Can you explain the cache part again? we use Redis for session state now.
[01:02] Marcus: Sure. The KV cache I'm saying is the model-side key/value cache for attention; it stays resident per session to avoid recomputing previous tokens. It's not Redis, it's internal cache on the serving runtime. If you need session storage for metadata you still use Redis or your DB.
[01:18] Sara: Ok good. Our concern is latency spikes — we need 200ms p95 on short prompts.
[01:24] Marcus: Understood. Two levers: pick lower-latency model variants and tune generation params. Also use our console Optimize suggestions to pick quantization/profile that reduces per-token latency. For short prompts trimming max_tokens and using streaming low-latency kernels helps.
[01:40] Marcus: Quick demo, I'm hitting the sandbox conversation endpoint. Notice streaming frames arrive every ~50-100ms depending on batch aggregation.
[01:51] [sound of typing]
[01:55] Marcus: Example payload: temperature 0.2, top_p 0.9, max_output_tokens 64. The response shows partial text arrives within 120ms for a 12-token reply.
[02:06] Devon: What about concurrency? we sometimes have spikes of 200 concurrent users.
[02:11] Marcus: On Hosted API we do autoscaling; you can also reserve Dedicated capacity if you want deterministic throughput. For spikes, our smart routing will spill to compatible variants or regions if configured.
[02:23] Marta: On compliance — where does data persist? logs, KV cache etc. We need SOC2 and KMS details.
[02:31] Lydia: We'll share the security pack, but short answer: ephemeral runtime caches are not persisted to disk long-term; request/response logs can be configured to be disabled or routed to your VPC in Private mode. We support customer-managed KMS for keys.
[02:44] Marta: Do you support SAML SSO and role-based access?
[02:48] Lydia: Yes SAML and SCIM provisioning, RBAC, and audit logs. We'll drop the compliance docs after the call.
[02:56] Marcus: Back to retries: streaming and retries interplay is important. If a streaming connection drops mid-response we support resume tokens for short windows and idempotency keys for completely restarting the generation. Our SDKs expose a retry helper that will attempt resume first, then fallback to a shorter variant.
[03:14] Devon: Resume tokens — do we need to store anything?
[03:18] Marcus: No, resume tokens are server-generated and returned in the last frame; client should pass them in the next request within TTL. If you want total idempotency you can also provide an idempotency key tied to your higher-level convo id.
[03:31] Sara: If resume fails, what's the observable: duplicate tokens or partial content?
[03:36] Marcus: You'll either get the resume continuation (preferred) or a restarted stream. Our retry policy tries resume then restart with the same seed when possible; duplicates are deduped on the SDK layer when we can. There are edge cases if you intentionally truncated earlier.
[03:49] Marta: Any PII retention by default?
[03:52] Lydia: By default we do not retain user content for hosted trials more than 30 days, and we have retention controls; for enterprise you can pick no retention and route logs to your vault.
[04:03] Devon: Show us a failure mode where streaming connection is flaky?
[04:07] Marcus: Sure — I'll throttle the websocket.
[04:11] [typing, simulated network throttling effect on the stream]
[04:18] Marcus: See the pause then resumed frame with a resume token. The console shows the token in the last chunk.
[04:26] Devon: Nice. How do we wire that into our headless client?
[04:29] Marcus: Small code snippet: client.openStream(conversationId, {idempotencyKey, resumeToken}), and the SDK will call retry strategies: exponential backoff with jitter, then fallback to alternate model variant if configured.
[04:42] Sara: Can you talk about cost? Lowering temperature vs max_tokens — what's the biggest lever?
[04:48] Marcus: Max_tokens and model family are biggest. Temperature only affects sampling randomness; it doesn't change token count. Use smaller model family or apply prefix/KV caching to save recomputation across repeated prompts. Optimize will recommend batching or cache warmup if patterns permit.
[05:05] Devon: Does Optimize automate batching or just suggest config?
[05:09] Priya (Product): Optimize will surface suggestions (e.g., batch size 8, quantize int8) and can produce a config snippet you can apply. It also shows expected token-cost delta and latency tradeoff for your profile.
[05:22] Sara: For our timeline — we want a pilot in 2 weeks and decision in a month. Is that realistic?
[05:28] Lydia: Yes, typical pilot is 2–4 weeks. We'll deliver sandbox creds and Marcus will run a benchmark with your sample dataset.
[05:36] Marta: About encryption in transit and at rest?
[05:39] Lydia: TLS 1.2/1.3 in transit, at-rest encryption via AWS KMS by default; you can plug customer-managed KMS in Private. We'll include HSM details for Dedicated.
[05:50] Devon: Any gotchas for our Go backend? we use a serverless frontend that proxies to our API.
[05:56] Marcus: Use our streaming SDK or the HTTP chunked responses; ensure you set an idempotency key on retries and handle partial responses — the SDK helpers do that for you. Also watch for client connection timeouts; we recommend 2x expected p95.
[06:10] Sara: Let's simulate a roundtrip benchmark — can you walk through the steps you'd run?
[06:14] Marcus: We'll ask for a representative prompt list (Devon), run 1k requests through the sandbox, measure p50/p95, and test with resume drop simulation. I'll post the raw CSV in the shared drive.
[06:28] Devon: Great. Any limits on streaming length? we sometimes do long summaries ~2k tokens.
[06:33] Marcus: We support long-context models; the runtime has attention optimizations but you may need to tune the chunking and KV cache. Long outputs increase cost and latency; Optimize can recommend quantization and batching to help.
[06:47] Marta: For legal, we'll need a data processing addendum and log retention SLA.
[06:52] Lydia: Noted. We'll route that to legal and include the DPA template.
[06:57] [brief cross-talk]
[07:05] Marcus: Quick tip: to reduce latency spikes, you can pin a warm pool (Dedicated) or use pre-warmed instances for peak hours. There's a small extra charge but helps p99.
[07:17] Devon: If we start with Hosted and then want Private, how much rework?
[07:21] Lydia: Minimal — API is identical; you'll reconfigure networking and keys. We'll help migrate conversation IDs and any internal tooling mapping.
[07:31] Sara: Ok wrapping up, any open concerns?
[07:34] Marta: I want the KMS/HSM and retention docs.
[07:37] Lydia: We'll send those.
[07:39] Devon: Benchmark timeline?
[07:40] Marcus: I'll run it by 8/20.
[07:43] Lydia: I'll shoot the pricing and pilot contract options by Friday 8/15.
[07:48] Marcus: Any final product notes: the Console shows per-route token split, model fallbacks and Optimize suggestions. I'll attach a short console GIF and the sample curl requests.
[07:59] Sara: Sounds good, thanks.
[08:01] Lydia: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with next steps.

Notes: occasional transcription artifacts: "KV cash" heard in recording as "KV cache"; some acronyms mis-transcribed.
